13 At sea level, atmospheric pressure is 100 kPa and the density of air is 1.3 kg m–3.
Assume that the density of air decreases linearly with height above sea level.
What is an estimate of the total height of the atmosphere based on this information?
A
7.8 km
B
16 km
C
77 km
D
150 km

hints: Notice that the $100 \text{ kPa}$ pressure at sea level equals the total weight per unit area of the air column above it.
Because density decreases linearly from $1.3 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ to zero at the top, the average density for the whole column is half the sea-level value.
Set $p = \text{average density} \times g \times H$ with $g \approx 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and rearrange for $H$, then check the result in $\text{km}$.
walkthrough: Identify the physics: sea-level pressure supports the weight of air above $1 \text{ m}^2$, so $p = W/A = m g / A = \rho_{avg} H g$.
Use the linear decrease: density is $1.3 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ at the base and $0$ at height $H$, so the average is $\rho_{avg} = 1.3/2 = 0.65 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.
Rearrange for height: $H = p/(\rho_{avg} g) = 2p/(\rho_0 g)$.
Substitute with units: $H = 2 \times 100000 / (1.3 \times 9.81)$ where pressure is in $\text{Pa}$ and density in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$.
Calculate: $H \approx 200000 / 12.75 \approx 15700 \text{ m} \approx 16 \text{ km}$, which checks as $\text{m}$ from $\text{Pa}/(\text{kg m}^{-3} \times \text{m s}^{-2})$. This is option B.

A.explanation: This uses $p = \rho_0 g H$ with full sea-level density, giving about $7.8 \text{ km}$. It ignores that density falls linearly to zero so the average density is only half.

B.explanation: Using average density $\rho_0/2$ gives $p = (\rho_0/2) g H$, so $H \approx 16 \text{ km}$, matching the weight of the air column.

C.explanation: About $77 \text{ km}$ is far too large and would give a sea-level pressure about five times the given $100 \text{ kPa}$ even with the correct average density.

D.explanation: About $150 \text{ km}$ is roughly ten times too large and would imply a much heavier air column than $100 \text{ kPa}$ can support.
